chapter_title: Introduction to Smart Contracts and Solidity Basics

screens.title: Introduction to Smart Contracts and Solidity Basics
screens.subtitle: Why code on the blockchain is immutable, deterministic, and trustless — and how Solidity makes that possible.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn what a smart contract actually is, why immutability and determinism matter, and how Solidity lets you write executable, on-chain programs. Start by thinking of a smart contract as code that lives on the blockchain and runs automatically when conditions are met. That code becomes immutable after deployment, so you must test and audit carefully before you go live. Solidity is the high-level language we use to express that behavior for the Ethereum Virtual Machine. You will see how a contract is declared, how state variables store persistent data, and how functions change or read that state. We will walk through a simple storage example and a MessageBoard exercise you can try in Remix. Along the way I’ll highlight common beginner mistakes like choosing the wrong integer size or exposing a function unintentionally with an incorrect visibility modifier. By the end you will understand the core vocabulary and be ready to write and compile a basic contract in Remix. Consider: if code is permanent, what safeguards will you add before you deploy?

keyIdea.title: Smart contracts are code that becomes an immutable rule-set on-chain.
keyIdea.text: They execute deterministically across nodes and are authored in languages like Solidity that compile to EVM bytecode.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to practical competencies you will build while working through the chapter. First, you will be able to define a smart contract and list its distinguishing properties — immutability, determinism, transparency, and trustlessness. That definition helps you reason about risks and guarantees when you deploy code. Second, you will understand why Solidity is used to write EVM programs, what makes it contract-oriented, and how high-level constructs compile down to bytecode. Third, you will identify basic Solidity data types such as unsigned and signed integers, address, boolean, string, and bytes, and appreciate gas tradeoffs when choosing types. Finally, you will read and write simple contracts: declare state variables, add a constructor, and implement functions with appropriate visibility. Each objective pairs a conceptual claim with a short practical example so you can both explain and apply the ideas. Consider which of these objectives is most unfamiliar to you now and plan to revisit that section while coding in Remix.

screens.title: What is a Smart Contract?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and the properties that distinguish it from traditional contracts

narration.text: A smart contract is executable code deployed on a blockchain that enforces rules automatically. Define it succinctly as a self-executing, immutable, and deterministic agreement encoded in software. Immutability means once the contract is deployed its code cannot be changed, so the rules you program are permanent. Determinism means that given the same input on any node in the network, the contract produces the same output; this is essential for consensus. Transparency follows because public contracts have their code visible on-chain, enabling community audit. Trustlessness means users do not need to trust a central party; the blockchain enforces execution. A concrete example: a simple escrow that releases funds only when both parties signal completion. A common misconception is assuming immutability implies perfection — in fact, bugs remain on-chain unless off-chain governance or upgrade patterns were included from the start. Key takeaway: design conservatively, test extensively, and prefer minimal, well-audited code for core financial logic. How would you reduce risk if a contract holds large balances? What is a Smart Contract? means their immutability and determinism make them reliable but make careful design and testing mandatory.. In practical terms, a precise definition and the properties that distinguish it from traditional contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Smart contracts are permanent programmatic rules
keyIdea.text: Their immutability and determinism make them reliable but make careful design and testing mandatory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is a Smart Contract?
Definition

Smart Contract

A self-executing program deployed on a blockchain that enforces rules without a central authority.

Immutability

Once deployed, code cannot be altered. This ensures predictable behavior but requires rigorous pre-deployment checks.

Determinism

Same input yields same output across all nodes, which is essential for network consensus.

Transparency

Public contracts can be audited by anyone to verify logic and trustworthiness.

Trustlessness

Participants interact without trusting a central party because the blockchain enforces execution.

Concrete Example
Escrow example

Two parties deposit funds and the contract releases them only when both provide confirmation. The rule is enforced automatically and is immutable once deployed.

Common Mistake

Assuming immutability alone prevents all failures. Bugs can be permanent without built-in upgrade or governance patterns.

Key Takeaway

Design minimal trusted logic for any on-chain contract and validate behavior extensively before deployment.

screens.title: Solidity and the EVM
screens.subtitle: How Solidity maps contract-oriented code to EVM bytecode and why compiler version matters

narration.text: Solidity is a statically typed, contract-oriented language designed for writing programs that run on the Ethereum Virtual Machine. When you write a contract using the contract keyword and state variables and functions, the Solidity compiler translates that high-level code into EVM bytecode that is stored on-chain. Choosing a compiler version matters because language features, security checks, and gas optimizations evolve between versions. For example, Solidity versions starting with the eight series include built-in checks that prevent certain classes of arithmetic vulnerabilities. A concrete example is writing a SimpleStorage contract that declares a storedData unsigned integer and a setter function; the compiler will generate a constructor and bytecode to persist state. A common misconception is to assume high-level behavior is free: in reality, storage operations and dynamic types like string or bytes incur gas. Key takeaway: always pin a compatible compiler version, compile locally or in Remix, and inspect the compiled artifacts to understand gas and deployment size. Solidity and the EVM means compiler versions change behavior and safety checks; pin a version and inspect compiled output to reason about gas.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture

High-level → Bytecode

Solidity source is compiled into EVM bytecode which executes deterministically on each node.

Compiler version

Pinning the pragma ensures consistent behavior and includes version-specific safety fixes and gas improvements.

Gas implications

Storage writes and dynamic types are expensive; reviewing compiled artifacts helps you estimate deployment cost.

Example
SimpleStorage pattern

Declare an unsigned integer state variable, initialize it in a constructor, and provide a setter. The compiler will create a getter for public state.

Misconception

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Solidity Contract Structure — SimpleStorage Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A stepwise view of a minimal contract: state, constructor, setter and implicit getter

narration.text: Let's step through a minimal storage contract to connect language features to runtime behavior. The contract declares a state variable named storedData of an unsigned integer type. A constructor runs once on deployment to initialize storedData with a default value. A public setter function accepts a value and assigns it to storedData, changing the contract’s persistent state. Because the state variable is public, the compiler also generates an automatic getter that returns the current storedData. Practically, you will compile, deploy to the JavaScript VM, call the setter, and then call the getter to verify the state persisted. A common beginner mistake is using a small integer size like uint8 for values that can exceed its maximum; that produces overflow logic errors before Solidity introduced built-in safety checks in later compiler versions. Key takeaway: map each source-level line to its effect on storage, constructor execution, and runtime calls to avoid surprises at deployment. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › SimpleStorage Walkthrough
Code Walkthrough

SimpleStorage — core parts

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
    uint256 public storedData;

    constructor() {
        storedData = 100;
    }

    function set(uint256 x) public {
        storedData = x;
    }
}
State

storedData is stored persistently on-chain and reads cost less than writes.

Constructor

Runs once at deployment to initialize storedData to a default value.

Functions

set modifies state and is callable by anyone because it is public.

Concrete Example

Deploy on the JavaScript VM, call set with a new value, then confirm the getter returns the updated number. This proves persistence across calls.

Misconception

Beware of assuming public state means the variable is modifiable only by the owner; public only creates a reader plus exposes setter visibility if you declare one.

Try this

Change storedData type to uint8 and observe behavior when you set a value larger than 255 to see overflow checks in your chosen compiler version.

screens.title: Basic Solidity Data Types
screens.subtitle: Understanding uint, int, address, bool, string, and bytes and gas tradeoffs

narration.text: Solidity provides several fundamental types you will use in nearly every contract. Unsigned integers, written as uint with an optional bit width like 256, hold non-negative numbers. Signed integers, int variants, include negative values. The address type is a 20-byte identifier for externally owned accounts or other contracts and is essential when tracking ownership or sending value. Boolean values represent true or false logic. Strings are dynamically-sized UTF‑8 sequences and are convenient for text but relatively expensive to store. The bytes family includes dynamic bytes and fixed-size bytes1 through bytes32; fixed-size bytes are more gas-efficient than strings when storing raw binary-like data. A concrete example: storing a wallet address and a small flag uses address and bool which are compact, whereas storing long messages uses string and will raise gas costs. A common misconception is that smaller integer widths always save gas — in some contexts the EVM operates most efficiently with 256-bit words, so measure and pick types based on actual gas profiles. Key takeaway: choose types deliberately and consider storage cost for each decision. Basic Solidity Data Types means use address and bool for compact storage, prefer fixed-size bytes for binary, and measure gas when choosing integer widths.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Basic Data Types

Common Types

Understand the type, its purpose, and cost considerations when storing it on-chain.

uint / int

Unsigned and signed integers with bit widths from 8 to 256. Use the smallest safe size but measure gas; 256-bit words are often natural for the EVM.

address

20-byte identifier for accounts or contracts. Use it to record ownership or send value securely with checks.

bool

Boolean flags for simple conditions. Pack multiple booleans into a single word when possible to save gas.

string / bytes

Strings are dynamic and costly. bytes and fixed-size bytes are more efficient for raw data.

Concrete Scenario
Message board choices

To store a message, string is practical but increases gas. For short fixed-length tokens, bytes32 may be cheaper.

Misconception

Smaller bit widths always save gas. Not always—packing and word alignment matter. Measure in your environment.

Key Takeaway

Choose types to balance correctness, readability, and gas. Test storage cost in Remix or with local tools.

screens.title: Function Visibility Modifiers
screens.subtitle: Public, private, internal, external — who can call a function and when to use each

narration.text: Function visibility determines who can invoke a function and influences gas patterns and inheritance. Public functions are callable both externally via transactions and internally from other functions. They are the default choice for simple setters and actions intended for user interaction. Private functions are only callable from within the contract where they are defined; derived contracts and external callers cannot access them. Internal functions are similar to private but allow access from derived contracts, enabling safe code reuse in inheritance hierarchies. External functions can only be called from other contracts or transactions; calling an external function internally requires a different call form and may be slightly more gas efficient for interface-like operations. A concrete example: marking a helper function private prevents accidental external invocation, while marking an A P I entry point external encourages efficient external usage. A common confusion is assuming public and external are interchangeable; they are not. Key takeaway: pick visibility to enforce access rules and gas expectations, and test access patterns to confirm your intended protection. Function Visibility Modifiers means use private/internal to restrict access, public for general access, and external for external-only interface functions.. In practical terms, public, private, internal, external — who can call a function and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Visibility enforces access and affects gas
keyIdea.text: Use private/internal to restrict access, public for general access, and external for external-only interface functions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Function Visibility
Modifiers

Who can call a function?

public
Callable externally and internally. Useful for API functions and setters.
private
Only callable inside the declaring contract. Not visible to derived contracts or external callers.
internal
Callable within the contract and by derived contracts. Good for inheritance-safe helpers.
external
Callable only from external accounts or other contracts, not via internal calls in the same contract using simple calls.
Concrete Example
Helper vs API

Mark internal/private for internal helpers, and external/public for exposed API endpoints. This prevents unintended external access to internal functions.

Misconception

Confusing public and external. They differ in internal call semantics and gas profile; test to confirm desired behavior.

Key Takeaway

Set visibility deliberately to enforce access control, reduce mistakes, and favor gas-efficient patterns where applicable.

screens.title: MessageBoard Hands-on in Remix
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step instructions and reasoning for implementing owner checks and interacting with the contract

narration.text: This walkthrough shows a practical pattern: building a MessageBoard contract, compiling it, and adding an ownership check to the setter. Start by creating a new file in Remix and declaring your contract with two state variables: a string for the message and an address for the owner. In the constructor set the message to a default greeting and set owner to the deploying address using msg. sender. When you implement the setMessage function, add a require statement that checks msg. sender equals owner, returning a clear error message if the caller is not authorized. This pattern prevents unauthorized changes while keeping logic simple and auditable. After implementing the require check, compile again and deploy to the JavaScript VM. Call setMessage as the owner to see the update, then attempt the same call from another account to verify the require blocks it. Common mistakes include forgetting to mark the owner variable public if you want to read it off-chain, or using the wrong visibility on setMessage. Key takeaway: ownership checks are a first-line defense — test both success and failure paths to be confident before deployment.

keyIdea.title: Ownership checks prevent unintended updates
keyIdea.text: Use msg.sender comparisons in require statements to restrict state-changing calls to an owner or authorized account.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › MessageBoard in Remix
Step-by-step

Implement and verify owner-restricted setter

// MessageBoard (starter)
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MessageBoard {
    string public currentMessage;
    address public owner;

    constructor() {
        currentMessage = "Hello Cohortia!";
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    function setMessage(string memory _newMessage) public {
        // require check to ensure only owner can set the message
        currentMessage = _newMessage;
    }
}
Add require

Insert a require that msg.sender equals owner with an explanatory message to enforce owner-only updates.

Deploy and test

Deploy to the JavaScript VM, call setMessage from the deploying account, then from another account to observe the require failure.

Concrete Check

After adding require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the contract owner can set the message."), test both success and failure paths to validate access control.

Misconception

Leaving the require out or using an incorrect comparison allows unauthorized users to change state unexpectedly.

Try this

Make owner private and add a public getter only if you want read access without exposing a writable slot; reflect on tradeoffs.

screens.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Integer sizing, visibility errors, and skipping tests — why they matter and how to avoid them

narration.text: Beginners often stumble on a few recurring mistakes that lead to costly bugs. First, integer sizing errors: choosing an overly small unsigned integer such as a uint8 for values that can exceed 255 can lead to unexpected behavior or arithmetic issues. While recent Solidity versions add safety checks, always select a size that fits the domain and test boundary conditions. Second, incorrect function visibility can expose internal helpers or leave setters callable by anyone; picking public by accident or misusing external versus public produces functional and gas consequences. Third, skipping tests and audits before deployment is dangerous because on-chain immutability prevents simple fixes. A practical mitigation is to use the JavaScript VM for iterative testing, add require checks for critical paths, and separately peer-review contract logic. A final common pitfall is storing large strings or dynamic arrays on-chain without considering gas; compress or move large off-chain content when possible. Key takeaway: anticipate edge cases, assert critical conditions, and verify both success and failure paths in tests before deploying. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Common Beginner Mistakes

Frequent pitfalls and mitigations

Integer sizing

Choose an integer width that fits your domain, and test boundary values to avoid overflow or unintended truncation.

Visibility errors

Accidentally exposing internal functions or leaving setters open creates security and correctness problems.

No tests before deploy

Because contracts are immutable, testing on local VMs and code review are essential safeguards.

Practical checks
Test both success and failure paths

Include tests that trigger require failures and boundary conditions so you fully understand behavior before deployment.

Gas consideration

Move large content off-chain or store hashes on-chain to reduce cost when you must preserve integrity without storing bulky data.

Key Takeaway

Mitigate risk with conservative types, clear visibility, require assertions, and local testing before any mainnet deployment.

screens.title: Testing and Deployment Workflow
screens.subtitle: Compile, deploy to JavaScript VM, interact, then plan for audits and mainnet deployment

narration.text: A disciplined workflow reduces the chance of costly mistakes. Begin locally: compile your contract in Remix and fix any warnings. Deploy repeatedly to the JavaScript VM to iterate quickly on constructor values and function behavior. Interact with setters and getters, and verify that state changes persist across calls. Add require statements for critical access checks and write small test cases that assert both successful updates and rejected calls. After local validation, prepare an artifact bundle of source, ABI, and compiler version for review. Then perform a code audit or peer review focused on access control, arithmetic safety, and gas-heavy operations. Only after tests and reviews are clean should you deploy to a live network, and even then consider deploying minimal upgradeable patterns or proxy scaffolds only if you understand upgrade risks. A common misconception is to rush to mainnet after a few manual checks; automated tests and peer reviews catch issues manual interactions miss. Key takeaway: invest time in tests and reviews; immutability makes pre-deployment work pay dividends. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Testing & Deployment Workflow

Verification steps before mainnet

1. Compile & inspect

Fix warnings and pin the pragma to ensure reproducible builds.

2. Local VM testing

Deploy to the JavaScript VM, test setters and getters, and validate require paths.

3. Automated tests

Add tests that assert both success and failure cases; include edge values for integers and access checks.

4. Audit and review

Peer review for access control, reentrancy, and gas pitfalls. Collect artifacts for reproducibility.

5. Plan deployment

Consider small staged deployments, and document upgrade pathways only if necessary and audited.

Key Takeaway

A repeatable workflow of compile, test, audit, and staged deploy reduces risk given immutability.

screens.title: Practical Example: Gas and Storage Tradeoffs
screens.subtitle: Why storing strings or large arrays on-chain costs and alternatives to consider

narration.text: Storing data on-chain is powerful but costly. Dynamic types such as strings and dynamic bytes allocate storage that increases gas consumption for deployment and for each state write. For example, a MessageBoard that stores long messages will cost significantly more to update than a contract that only stores a short bytes32 hash. A practical alternative is to store a hash on-chain and keep the full content off-chain, retrieving it via an indexing or storage network. Another tradeoff is packing multiple small variables into a single storage slot to save gas, which requires careful ordering of state variables. A common misconception is that more compact types always reduce gas; sometimes using 256-bit aligned words is more efficient in the EVM. Key takeaway: measure gas cost for representative inputs, consider off-chain storage for bulky content, and design state layout intentionally to minimize repeated expensive writes. Practical Example: Gas and Storage Tradeoffs means prefer compact state for frequently updated data and keep large or mutable content off-chain, storing hashes on-chain when necessary.. In practical terms, why storing strings or large arrays on-chain costs and alternatives to consider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Store only what must be on-chain
keyIdea.text: Prefer compact state for frequently updated data and keep large or mutable content off-chain, storing hashes on-chain when necessary.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Gas & Storage Tradeoffs

Costly vs cheap storage

Dynamic data like strings or arrays cost more to store and update. Use hashes or off-chain storage when possible.

On-chain hash pattern

Store a hash on-chain, keep large content off-chain, and verify integrity using the hash when needed.

Storage packing

Order variables to pack multiple small types into a single 256-bit slot to reduce storage cost.

Scenario
MessageBoard optimization

Instead of storing long messages, store a content hash and display full messages from an off-chain source validated against the on-chain hash.

Misconception

Assuming fixed-size types are always cheaper. Aligning with EVM word size can be more efficient depending on operations and access patterns.

Key Takeaway

Measure gas for representative inputs and prefer storing only the minimal necessary on-chain to balance cost and security.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders you should retain from this chapter

narration.text: Keep three practical concepts in mind as you build smart contracts. First, immutability and determinism mean deployed code is permanent and produces the same result across nodes; design conservatively and test thoroughly. Second, Solidity is the high-level language for the EVM; pin your compiler version, understand that state variables live on-chain, and remember compilation produces bytecode that determines gas cost. Third, choose types and visibility deliberately: use address and bool for compact storage, prefer fixed-size bytes when appropriate, and set function visibility to enforce intended access. A short practice: implement the MessageBoard in Remix, add a require that only the owner can set the message, and test both allowed and rejected calls. These three ideas reduce deployment risk and give you a solid foundation for more advanced topics. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three concise reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Keep this short reference to guide your next coding session. First, remember the core characteristics: immutability, determinism, transparency, and trustlessness. Second, recall that Solidity is statically typed and compiles to bytecode — pin your pragma and inspect compiled output. Third, always reason about storage and visibility: choose types deliberately, add require checks for authorization, and test both allowed and blocked calls. Ask yourself after each change: could this be exploited or cost more gas than I expect? This mindset will make your first contracts safer and easier to maintain. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means immutability matters, compiler version matters, and type/visibility choices matter.. In practical terms, three concise reminders to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
